name: Thyroid blood tests: TSH and T4 explained
summary: Thyroid tests read TSH and free T4 together: a high TSH with low T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, and the reverse an overactive one.
keyPoints: TSH is the most sensitive marker of thyroid status, and it is read together with free T4.
A high TSH with a low free T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, and a low TSH with a high free T4 suggests an overactive thyroid.
A slightly raised TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism and is followed over time.
Severe illness and some medicines can change thyroid results without a thyroid disease.

body.heading: What do TSH and T4 show?
body.body: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes thyroid hormones. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, or TSH, comes from the pituitary gland and tells the thyroid how much hormone to make. The British Thyroid Foundation calls TSH the most sensitive marker of thyroid status. T4 is the main thyroid hormone, and doctors usually look at free T4, the part not bound to proteins. Results are read as a pattern of TSH and free T4 together, not one number alone.

body.heading: What pattern suggests an underactive thyroid?
body.body: A high TSH with a low free T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, called hypothyroidism. The NHS says a blood test measuring hormone levels is the only accurate way to find out whether there is a problem. A GP will also ask about symptoms and may examine the neck. Thyroid UK says a low free T4 with a raised TSH will usually give a diagnosis of hypothyroidism.

body.heading: What pattern suggests an overactive thyroid?
body.body: The reverse pattern, a low TSH with a high free T4, suggests an overactive thyroid, called hyperthyroidism. The NHS describes blood tests as part of how an overactive thyroid is diagnosed.

body.heading: What if the results are borderline?
body.body: A slightly raised TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism. It may gradually develop into clinical hypothyroidism over many years. A test for thyroid antibodies helps to judge that risk. Thyroid UK says there is no evidence that routine early treatment helps when the TSH is only a little above the reference range. A low TSH with a low free T4 may come from a problem with the pituitary gland, or from a significant illness that does not involve the thyroid.

body.heading: Can illness or medicines change the result?
body.body: Abnormal T4 levels do not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Severe illness and some medicines, such as birth control pills and steroids, can affect T4 levels.

body.heading: What happens after a diagnosis?
body.body: Underactive thyroid is usually treated with daily hormone replacement tablets called levothyroxine. The NHS says this treatment is long term to prevent symptoms. NHS inform says a mild case with no symptoms may not need treatment. Regular blood tests check that the dose is right, because a wrong dose can cause side effects such as feeling sick, diarrhoea, headaches or problems sleeping. For people on replacement, TSH is the main test used to check that the treatment is adequate.

body.heading: What can cause an underactive or overactive thyroid?
body.body: In the UK the main cause of an underactive thyroid is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's disease. Damage to the thyroid during treatment for an overactive thyroid or thyroid cancer is another cause. Common symptoms of an underactive thyroid include tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold, constipation and low mood, and they develop slowly. Graves' disease is the most common cause of an overactive thyroid. Symptoms of an overactive thyroid include nervousness, weight loss despite a good appetite, a fast or irregular heartbeat, tremor and sleep difficulty. Treatment for an overactive thyroid can include anti-thyroid medicines, beta-blockers for symptoms such as tremor, and radioactive iodine. Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid afterwards. In Graves' disease, blood tests look for antibodies as well as hormone levels.
